title: Why Do Water Drops Dance on a Hot Pan?
pause_note: 'long' lists beat indices followed by a 1.5 s pause; Short: keep pauses to 0.6 s

beats: Why do water drops dance on a really hot pan?
On a hot pan, a drop of water hisses and is gone in a moment.
On a hotter pan, it skates around for over a minute.
Hotter, yet it lasts longer. How?
Above roughly two hundred degrees Celsius, depending on the pan, the bottom of the drop boils the instant it lands.
That steam is trapped underneath: a cushion about as thin as a hair.
The drop floats. It never touches the metal.
Steam carries heat poorly, so the cushion shields the drop from the pan.
With nothing to rub against, it glides.
This is the Leidenfrost effect, named after a doctor who wrote about it in 1756.
Cool the pan, the cushion collapses, and the drop boils away.
So what else could float on its own steam?
